questions.prompt: What is a selection rate for a group?
options: The group's share of the dataset
questions.explanation: Selection rate is how often the model predicts positive for that group, regardless of the true label.

questions.prompt: A good overall accuracy can hide large performance gaps between groups.
questions.explanation: True. Reporting only overall accuracy is a listed mistake; disaggregate by group and slice.

questions.prompt: Which is a proxy feature that can reintroduce bias after removing a protected attribute?
questions.explanation: Postcode or school can correlate with protected attributes, so dropping the attribute does not guarantee fairness.

questions.prompt: What is the equalized odds difference?
questions.code:
group A: TPR = 0.80, FPR = 0.10
group B: TPR = 0.70, FPR = 0.30
questions.explanation: TPR gap = 0.80 - 0.70 = 0.10; FPR gap = 0.30 - 0.10 = 0.20. Fairlearn's equalized odds difference is the larger of the two: 0.20.

questions.prompt: Group A has 12 applicants and group B has 4,000. Group A's selection rate is 0.25 vs 0.40. What should you be careful about?
options: Small samples make group A's rate noisy; report uncertainty (intervals) and avoid strong conclusions either way
questions.explanation: Ignoring sample size is a listed mistake; a small group's noisy rate can drive wrong conclusions.

questions.prompt: Why can't a typical imperfect classifier satisfy demographic parity and equalized odds at the same time when base rates differ?
options: When groups have different base rates, equal selection rates and equal error rates generally conflict, so a definition must be chosen deliberately
Because both metrics are the same
questions.explanation: Different base rates make the criteria mathematically incompatible for non-perfect classifiers; choose and document the definition based on harm.

questions.prompt: A counterfactual test swaps a name on 50 CVs, runs once, and finds no difference. The team declares the screener fair. What is wrong?
options: LLM scores vary between runs, so run multiple samples and compare distributions; and a passing test is evidence about the tested cases, not proof of fairness
questions.explanation: Running counterfactual tests once and treating a pass as proof are both listed mistakes.

questions.prompt: A team wants to collect applicants' ethnicity to measure fairness. What must happen first?
options: Privacy and legal review of collection, purpose, storage and access
Add it as a model feature
questions.explanation: Collecting group data without privacy and legal review is a listed mistake, even when the purpose is fairness testing.

questions.prompt: Which NIST publication groups AI bias into systemic, statistical/computational and human categories?
questions.explanation: NIST SP 1270 provides that taxonomy. AI 600-1 is the Generative AI Profile; ISO/IEC 42001 is a management-system standard; SR 26-2 is US banking model risk guidance.

coding.title: Group selection rates and parity difference
coding.prompt: Write `parity(preds, groups)` where `preds` are 0/1 predictions and `groups` the group label for each row. Return `(rates, diff)`: a dict of group -> selection rate (rounded to 4 decimals) and the demographic parity difference (max rate - min rate, rounded to 4).
coding.explanation: Selection rate is positives over rows per group; the parity difference is the largest gap. Zero means equal selection rates, which is one, but not the only, fairness definition.
hints: Count rows and positive predictions per group.

coding.title: Equalized odds difference
coding.prompt: Write `equalized_odds_diff(y_true, y_pred, groups)` returning the larger of the TPR gap and the FPR gap across groups (max - min of each), rounded to 4 decimals. If a group has no positives (or no negatives), skip it for that rate.
coding.explanation: This mirrors Fairlearn's definition: equal opportunity looks only at the TPR gap; equalized odds also requires equal false positive rates and reports the worse of the two gaps.
hints: Per group, split predictions by the true label.
TPR is mean prediction among true positives; FPR among true negatives.
Return the larger of the two gaps.

tests.name: FPR gap dominates
tests.code:
yt=[1,1,0,0,1,1,0,0]
yp=[1,1,0,0,1,0,1,1]
g=['a']*4+['b']*4
assert equalized_odds_diff(yt,yp,g)==1.0, equalized_odds_diff(yt,yp,g)

tests.name: TPR gap only
tests.code:
yt=[1,1,0,1,1,0]
yp=[1,1,0,1,0,0]
g=['a','a','a','b','b','b']
assert equalized_odds_diff(yt,yp,g)==0.5, equalized_odds_diff(yt,yp,g)

coding.title: Counterfactual name-swap test
coding.prompt: Write `counterfactual_gaps(score_fn, template, names, runs, tolerance)`. For each name, fill `template` (containing `{name}`) and call `score_fn(text)` `runs` times; take the mean score per name. Return `(means, ok)` where `means` maps name -> mean rounded to 3 decimals and `ok` is True when max mean - min mean <= tolerance (with a 1e-9 slack).
coding.explanation: Counterfactual tests are metamorphic: only the name changes, so the score should not. Averaging several runs separates a real gap from run-to-run noise, which a single run cannot.
hints: Call the scorer `runs` times per name and average.
Compare the spread of means with the tolerance.

tests.name: Detects a biased scorer
tests.code:
def s(t):
    return 3.0 if 'Emily' in t else 4.0
m,ok=counterfactual_gaps(s,'CV of {name}: 5 years QA',['Emily','Greg'],3,0.2)
assert m=={'Emily':3.0,'Greg':4.0} and ok is False, (m,ok)

tests.name: Averages noisy runs
tests.code:
import itertools
seq=itertools.cycle([3.0,4.0])
m,ok=counterfactual_gaps(lambda t:next(seq),'{name}',['A','B'],2,0.1)
assert m=={'A':3.5,'B':3.5} and ok is True, (m,ok)
